messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 26
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Student
- Trauma Type: Toxic chemical exposure
- Pcl5: 70

# The Weight of the Air She Breathes

Valentina is twenty-six years old, a graduate student in environmental science — a choice she made, she says with a hollow laugh, because she wanted to understand the natural world. What she understands now is that the natural world can turn against you without warning, and that the body remembers things the mind would rather forget.

Two years ago, Valentina was working a part-time job at a commercial cleaning facility to help pay her tuition. It was supposed to be temporary. On an otherwise unremarkable Tuesday afternoon, a storage malfunction caused a pressurized tank of industrial solvent to rupture. The vapor spread through the ventilation system before anyone understood what was happening. Valentina remembers the smell first — something sharp and sweet that didn't belong — and then the burning that started in her throat and moved into her chest like a fist closing around her lungs. She remembers colleagues dropping to their knees. She remembers not being able to call for help because she couldn't form words. By the time emergency services arrived, she had lost consciousness. She spent four days in the hospital. Three of her coworkers were hospitalized as well. One, a woman named Rosa who had shared her lunch break most days, did not go home.

Valentina was discharged with a clean bill of physical health. She returned to her apartment, to her coursework, to her life — and found that none of it fit anymore.

She cannot tolerate enclosed spaces with poor ventilation. In the library where she used to spend entire afternoons, she now sits near the exit with her jacket on, measuring the distance to the door. When a classmate uncaps a marker or a professor uses cleaning spray on the whiteboard, something in Valentina's nervous system treats it as a catastrophe. Her heart accelerates. Her vision narrows. She has left seminars mid-sentence, standing in the hallway afterward with her hands pressed flat against the cool wall, trying to convince herself she is not dying.

At night, she rarely sleeps past three in the morning. When she does sleep, she is often back in the facility — the sweetness in the air, Rosa somewhere behind her, her own legs not working the way they should. She wakes with her chest heaving and lies in the dark cataloguing the smells of her apartment, reassuring herself one by one. She has begun sleeping with the window cracked even in winter.

Her dissertation research, which focuses on industrial pollutants in urban watersheds, has become both a compulsion and a torment. She is drawn to the material in a way she cannot fully articulate — as though understanding the chemistry of harm might give her some retroactive control over what happened to her. But reading case studies of chemical exposure sometimes sends her into a dissociative fog that lasts hours. She has missed two thesis meetings this semester without explanation, sitting in her car in the parking lot, unable to make herself go inside.

She describes herself as someone who has become difficult to be around. She has pulled away from her family — her mother calls every Sunday from Medellín, and Valentina answers in a voice she describes as borrowed, performing a version of herself that feels increasingly fictional. She has not told her mother what happened. She does not want to be the reason her mother worries from so far away.

What Valentina talks about most, in the quiet of the therapy room, is Rosa. She talks about the shared lunches. She talks about the fact that she was closer to the exit. She talks about the smell of the solvent as though it is still present, still moving through her, and in some fundamental way she believes it is — that something entered her that day that has not left, that the air she breathes now is never entirely clean, and that she is still, in some part of herself, waiting to find out whether she will survive it.
